explain.gdp_pc_taka: If everything Bangladesh produced in one year were shared equally among every person, each person's share would be {value}. It is not what people actually earn. It shows the size of the economy compared with the number of people.
explain.gdp_pc_ppp: The same measure, in international dollars. These adjust for the fact that the same things cost different amounts in different countries, so countries can be compared fairly.
explain.gdp_growth: How much larger (or smaller) the whole economy became compared with the year before, after removing the effect of price rises.
explain.gdp_pc_growth: How much each person's share of the economy grew or shrank in a year. It is the growth of the whole economy, adjusted for the change in the number of people.
explain.inflation: How much more a typical basket of goods and services costs than a year ago. At {value}%, what cost 100 taka a year ago costs about {value_plus_100} taka now.
explain.exchange_rate: How many taka are needed to buy one US dollar.
explain.unemployment: The share of people in the labour force who have no job but are looking for one. People who are not looking for work are not counted.
explain.youth_unemployment: The same measure, for people aged 15 to 24.
explain.female_lfp: The share of women aged 15 and older who are working or looking for work.
explain.remittances_gdp: Money sent home by Bangladeshis living abroad, compared with the size of the whole economy. At {value}%, it equals about {value} taka in every 100 taka the country produces.
explain.reserves_months: How many months of imports the country's foreign currency reserves could pay for.
explain.reserves_usd: Foreign currency and similar assets held by the central bank, shown in US dollars as published.
explain.poverty_intl: The share of people living on less than {line} a day, in prices adjusted for what money can buy in each country, so countries can be compared.
explain.poverty_lmic: The same idea, using a higher daily line of {line} that the World Bank uses for lower-middle-income countries.
explain.poverty_national: The share of people whose spending is below the poverty line set by Bangladesh itself. Other countries set their own lines, so this is not used to compare countries.
explain.gini: A number from 0 to 100 showing how unequally income or spending is shared. 0 means everyone has the same. 100 means one person has everything.
explain.share_low20: The share of all income (or spending) that goes to the poorest one-fifth of people.
explain.share_top10: The share of all income (or spending) that goes to the richest one-tenth of people.
explain.literacy: The share of people aged 15 and older who can read and write, with understanding, a short simple statement about everyday life.
explain.secondary_enrol: The number of students in secondary school as a share of children of secondary-school age. It can be above 100% because older or younger students are included.
explain.primary_completion: The share of children who reach the last year of primary school, compared with the number of children of the right age.
explain.pupil_teacher: The average number of primary school students for each teacher.
explain.edu_spend: How much the government spends on education, as a share of the whole economy.
explain.life_expectancy: The average number of years a baby born now would live if today's death rates stayed the same throughout their life.
explain.under5_mortality: How many children die before their fifth birthday, for every 1,000 children born alive.
explain.maternal_mortality: How many women die from causes linked to pregnancy or childbirth, for every 100,000 live births. This is a modelled estimate.
explain.stunting: The share of children under five whose height is too low for their age. It is used worldwide to measure long-term undernutrition.
explain.dpt: The share of one-year-old children who have had all three doses of the DPT vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough).
explain.physicians: The number of doctors for every 1,000 people.
explain.beds: The number of hospital beds for every 1,000 people.
explain.oop: Of every 100 taka spent on health care, about {value} taka are paid directly by people themselves, not by the government or insurance.
explain.health_spend_gdp: The total spent on health by government, households and others, as a share of the whole economy.

note.wb_national_accounts_fy: The reporting period for national accounts data is designated as either calendar year basis (CY) or fiscal year basis (FY). For this country, it is fiscal year-based (fiscal year-end: {month} {day}). Also, an estimate (PA.NUS.ATLS) of the exchange rate covers the same period and thus differs from the official exchange rate (CY).
note.wb_alternative_conversion: The World Bank systematically assesses the appropriateness of official exchange rates as conversion factors. In this country, multiple or dual exchange rate activity exists and must be accounted for appropriately in underlying statistics. An alternative estimate (“alternative conversion factor” - PA.NUS.ATLS) is thus calculated as a weighted average of the different exchange rates in use in the country. Doing so better reflects economic reality and leads to more accurate cross-country comparisons and country classifications by income level. For this country, this applies to the period {from}-{to}. Alternative conversion factors are used in the Atlas methodology and elsewhere in World Development Indicators as single-year conversion factors.

explain.gdp_total_taka: The value of everything produced in Bangladesh in one year, in taka.
explain.gdp_total_ppp: The same measure in international dollars. These adjust for the fact that the same things cost different amounts in different countries, so countries can be compared.
explain.electricity: The share of people who have access to electricity.
explain.safe_water: The share of people whose drinking water comes from a safe source at their home, is available when needed and is free from contamination.
explain.pm25: The average amount of very fine dust (PM2.5) in the air people breathe over a year, in micrograms per cubic metre of air.
explain.hdi_rank: The UN Development Programme's ranking of countries by its Human Development Index, which combines life expectancy, years of schooling and income. 1 is the highest index value.
explain.cpi_rank: Transparency International's ranking of countries by how corrupt experts and business people see their public sector to be. 1 is seen as the least corrupt.
explain.whr_rank: The World Happiness Report's ranking of countries by how people rate their own lives on a scale from 0 to 10, averaged over three years. 1 is the highest average.

sub.bangladesh_only: Figures in taka are published for Bangladesh only. To compare countries, the site uses international dollars:
sub.poverty-and-inequality.lede: How many people live below a poverty line, and how income or spending is shared.
sub.poverty-and-inequality.intro: A poverty line is an amount of money a day. The share of people below it is counted from household surveys, so figures exist only for survey years. Some countries measure income and others spending (consumption); each value says which. Bangladesh's national poverty line is set by Bangladesh itself, so it is shown for Bangladesh only.
sub.growth-and-prices.lede: The size of the economy for each person, how fast it changes, and how fast prices rise.
sub.growth-and-prices.intro: GDP is the value of everything produced in the country in a year. GDP per person divides it by the number of people. Growth compares one year with the year before, after removing price changes. Inflation is the yearly change in the prices of a typical basket of goods and services.
sub.jobs.lede: Who has work, and who is looking for it.
sub.jobs.intro: Unemployment counts people who have no job and are looking for one, as a share of everyone working or looking. People who are not looking for work are not counted. Labour force participation is the share of people who are working or looking for work.
sub.money-and-reserves.lede: Money sent home by Bangladeshis abroad, and the foreign currency the central bank holds.
sub.money-and-reserves.intro: Remittances are shown compared with the size of the economy. Reserves are shown as months of imports they could pay for, and in US dollars as published.

about.lede: What this site is, the rules it follows, and where its figures come from.
about.what.p1: Kemon Ache Bangladesh? (How is Bangladesh doing?) brings together published figures about life in Bangladesh: the economy, poverty and inequality, education and health. Each figure is shown next to the same figure for similar countries, in plain words, in English and Bangla.
about.what.p2: It is an independent project. It is not run by the World Bank, any other source it quotes, or any government office.
about.rules.p1: Only real, published figures. Nothing is estimated, filled in or forecast by this site. When a figure is missing, the site says "Data not available".
about.rules.p2: A source under every figure: the source's name with a link to the exact page, the year the figure is for, and the date it was retrieved.
about.rules.p3: No scores. The site never combines figures into one number. The only numbers it works out itself are simple sums, such as a difference, a rank among the countries shown, or a median; each is marked "Calculated by this site" with the values it used.
about.rules.p4: Neutral words. Figures are described as higher or lower, up or down. The site does not say whether a figure is good or bad, and does not say what caused it. Colours mark countries, not judgements.
about.rules.p5: Explanations are definitions. The short text under each measure says what the number means and links to the official definition.
about.data.p1: Most figures come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. The World Bank publishes the same measure, with the same definition, for almost every country, so countries can be compared fairly. Many of its figures come from other organisations, such as the UN, the World Health Organization, UNESCO, the International Labour Organization and the IMF; each figure's source line says which.
about.data.p2: Three published rankings are shown as their publishers give them: the UNDP Human Development Report, Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index, and the World Happiness Report.
about.data.p3: The figures are downloaded from the sources by a program and checked before they are published here. The date each figure was retrieved is under it, and the date of the latest check is at the foot of every page. The Sources page lists every figure with its links.
about.lang.p1: Every page is in both languages; the switch at the top changes between them. The sources publish in English, so names of reports and some notes from the sources are shown as published.
how.lede: A short guide to the parts of each page.
how.tile.p1: Each measure has a tile: its name, Bangladesh's latest figure, a short line saying what the figure means with a link to the official definition, and the source line.
how.tile.p2: Select the measure's name to open its own page, with every country to compare, Bangladesh over time, and where the figures come from.
how.years.p1: The data year is the year a figure describes. Many figures are published a year or more later, and survey figures only exist for survey years, so the data year is often earlier than this year.
how.years.p2: "Last checked", at the foot of every page, is the date the site last looked for new figures. A recent check does not mean the figures are recent.
how.peers.p1: The dots under a figure show the same measure for a set of similar countries, with Bangladesh in green. Each country's own data year is shown; when countries' years differ, a note says so.
how.peers.p2: The line marked "Median of lower-middle-income countries" is the middle value of all countries in that World Bank income group: half are above it and half below.
how.badge.p1: Only where an official goal, such as a UN Sustainable Development Goal, says which way a measure should move, a small badge says how many of the countries shown Bangladesh is ahead of or behind in that direction. The badge names the goal and links to it. Other measures get no badge.
how.calc.p1: A few numbers are worked out by the site from published figures: a median, a rank among countries, or a figure restated in one year's prices. Each is marked "Calculated by this site" and shows how it was worked out and the published values it used.
how.missing.p1: "Data not available" means the source has not published that figure. The site never fills the gap or shows a zero.
how.missing.p2: When the newest published figure is more than five years old, a note under it gives its year.
how.caveats.p1: Some figures come with a note from their source: for example, that a figure is a modelled estimate, or that a country measures income while another measures spending. These notes are shown next to the figure.
how.charts.p1: Every chart can be switched to a table with the Chart | Table switch, and its figures downloaded as a CSV file. In "Compare with other countries" you can add or remove countries, or pick a ready-made group.
how.money.p1: Money in Bangladesh is shown in taka where the source publishes taka. To compare countries, the site uses international dollars, which adjust for what money can buy in each country. Figures published only in US dollars are shown in US dollars. The site never converts between currencies itself.
how.lang.p1: In Bangla, numbers use Bangla digits and are grouped in lakh and crore.

note.p.emu_not_euros: Please note that historical data are not actual euros and are not comparable or suitable for aggregation across countries.
note.p.emu_not_euros_before: Please note that historical data before {before} are not actual euros and are not comparable or suitable for aggregation across countries.
note.p.germany_backward: GDP data before {year} are calculated by applying backward GDP growth rates of the former Federal Republic of Germany starting from the first official GDP value for the unified Germany ({year2}).
note.p.eurostat_reference: Based on data from EUROSTAT, the new reference year is {year}.
note.p.malta_sources: National accounts data source from {from} to {to} is Eurostat; prior to {before} is UN.
note.p.new_denomination: Data before {before} were adjusted to reflect the new denomination effective from {month} {day}, {year} ({code}), a decrease of {factor} times ({rate})
note.p.new_banknote: National account data were adjusted to reflect the new banknote ({rate})
note.p.zambia_kwacha: National accounts data were rebased to reflect the {month} {day}, {year}, introduction of the new Zambian kwacha at a rate of {old} old kwacha = {new} new kwacha.
note.p.zimbabwe_gold: National Accounts data are reported in Zimbabwe Gold (ZIG).
note.p.egypt_rebased: The national accounts data for Egypt has been updated to reflect local constant prices in the year {year}, moving from the previous reference of {old}.
note.p.revised_from_to: Authorities revised national accounts from {from} to {to}.
note.p.china_hk_macao: On {d1} July {y1} China resumed its exercise of sovereignty over Hong Kong, and on {d2} December {y2}, China resumed its exercise of sovereignty over Macao.
note.p.china_hk: On {day} July {year} China resumed its exercise of sovereignty over Hong Kong.
note.p.china_macao: On {day} December {year} China resumed its exercise of sovereignty over Macao.
note.p.china_excludes: Unless otherwise noted, data for China do not include data for Hong Kong SAR, China; Macao SAR, China; or Taiwan, China.
note.p.agri_mining: Agriculture value added includes mining and quarrying.
note.p.pvti: The source for national accounts data is the Pacific and Virgin Islands Training Initiative.
note.p.indonesia_timor: Data for Indonesia include Timor-Leste through {year} unless otherwise noted.
note.p.georgia_areas: Includes self-governed areas only, which mostly exclude Abkhazia and South Ossetia, but small areas in Abkhazia and South Ossetia are included before {y1} or {y2} because of the changes in self-governed areas.
note.p.cabinet_office: Classification for years after {after} was adjusted and figures were re-estimated by the World Bank, based on the detailed data published by the Cabinet Office, and are not consistent with data for {before} and before.
note.p.moldova_estimates: For {from}-{to}, World Bank estimates using UN World Population Prospects' growth rates of whole Moldova.
note.p.montenegro_independence: Montenegro declared independence from Serbia and Montenegro on {month} {day}, {year}.
note.p.shown_separately: Where available, data for each country are shown separately.
note.p.serbia_includes: However, for Serbia, some indicators continue to include data for Montenegro through {year}.
note.p.serbia_includes_long: However, for Serbia, some indicators, such as those series for which data appear only for Serbia and not Montenegro--e.g., aid, environment, external debt, balance of payments, various social indicators excluding population--continue to include data for Montenegro through {year}.
note.p.serbia_kosovo: Moreover, data from {year} onward for Serbia for most indicators exclude data for Kosovo, {year2} being the year when Kosovo became a territory under international administration pursuant to UN Security Council Resolution {res} ({year3}); any exceptions are noted.
note.p.kosovo_member: Kosovo became a World Bank member on {month} {day}, {year}; available data are shown separately for Kosovo.
note.p.serbia_methodology: In {year}, the Statistical Office of Serbia improved the methodology of national accounts data for {from} onward.
note.p.sectors_revised: Specifically, the classification of sectors was revised.
note.p.uruguay_npish: General Government final consumption expenditure includes Non-Profit Institutions Serving Households final concumption expenditure
note.p.venezuela_bcv: National Accounts data for the period {from}–{to} are sourced from the Central Bank of Venezuela.
note.p.venezuela_weo: Estimates for {from}–{to} are derived from the IMF World Economic Outlook (WEO), following methodological consultations with the IMF’s Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) and Statistics Departments.
note.p.venezuela_reviewed: Final estimates were reviewed by the World Bank Group's Prosperity Vertical.
indicator.sdg_rank.name: SDG Index, rank
explain.sdg_rank: The Sustainable Development Solutions Network's ranking of countries by its SDG Index, which measures overall progress toward the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals. 1 is the highest index value.
indicator.rsf_rank.name: World Press Freedom Index, rank
explain.rsf_rank: Reporters Without Borders' ranking of countries by how freely journalists can work, judged on political, economic, legal, social and safety conditions. 1 is the highest index value.
indicator.ghi_rank.name: Global Hunger Index, rank
explain.ghi_rank: The Global Hunger Index ranks countries by a hunger score built from undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting and child deaths. 1 is the lowest hunger score. Countries with very low scores share one rank.
source.name.rsf2026: Reporters Without Borders, World Press Freedom Index 2026
source.name.ghi2026: Global Hunger Index 2026 (Welthungerhilfe, Concern Worldwide, IFHV)
